claim: Spontaneous retinal waves are critical for the development of receptive fields in visual thalamus (LGN) and cortex (VC).
source: Spontaneous retinal waves are critical for the development of receptive fields in visual thalamus (LGN) and cortex (VC).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on retinal waves and receptive field development.

claim: During the period of retinal waves, corticothalamic connections excite LGN, rather than driving feedforward inhibition as observed in the adult.
source: During the period of retinal waves, corticothalamic connections excite LGN, rather than driving feedforward inhibition as observed in the adult.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation and pharmacological silencing experiments showing excitatory responses at P6-11 and inhibitory responses at P13-14.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback creates an excitatory feedback loop that gates retinal wave transmission through the LGN.
source: This creates an excitatory feedback loop that gates retinal wave transmission through the LGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that silencing VC reduces LGN activity by ~80%, similar to the reduction caused by retinal silencing.

claim: Cortical multiplication of retinal wave input ends just prior to eye-opening, as cortex begins to inhibit LGN.
source: This cortical multiplication of retinal wave input ends just prior to eye-opening, as cortex begins to inhibit LGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that at P13-14, VC silencing increases rather than decreases LGN activity, and optogenetic stimulation reveals post-stimulus inhibition.

claim: Prior to vision the retina generates waves of spontaneous firing that refine receptive field characteristics in visual thalamus and cortex.
source: For example, prior to vision the retina generates waves of spontaneous firing that refine receptive field characteristics in visual thalamus and cortex (Huberman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huberman et al., 2008.

claim: Retinal waves drive robust firing in LGN, superior colliculus, and VC.
source: Retinal waves drive robust firing in LGN, superior colliculus, and VC (Ackman and Crair, 2014) through a complex interaction between these structures (Weliky and Katz, 1999) that remains poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ackman and Crair, 2014.

claim: In the retina, transient circuit properties are responsible for wave propagation, most prominently hyper-connectivity of starburst amacrine cells.
source: In the retina, transient circuit properties are responsible for wave propagation, most prominently hyper-connectivity of starburst amacrine cells (Blankenship and Feller, 2010), but the degree to which the central transmission of retinal waves, or spontaneous activity in other systems, requires similar specializations is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blankenship and Feller, 2010.

claim: The relative amplification of ganglion cell spiking in developing thalamocortical circuits is approximately 40-fold that of the adult.
source: For example, the relative amplification of ganglion cell spiking in developing thalamocortical circuits is approximately 40-fold that of the adult (Colonnese et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colonnese et al., 2010.

claim: Preterm human neonates show sensory-evoked and spontaneous EEG events that reach amplitudes of over 1 millivolt, compared to microvolts in adults.
source: Evidence of similar amplification is observed in late second and early third trimester human neonates (born preterm), who show sensory-evoked and spontaneous EEG events that are paradoxically large, reaching amplitudes of over 1 millivolt, compared to microvolts in adults (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006.

claim: Strong neonatal activities persist despite low synaptic density (5–10% of the adult).
source: These strong neonatal activities persist despite low synaptic density (5–10% of the adult) (Aggelopoulos et al., 1989; Bourgeois and Rakic, 1993), weak individual synapses (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Etherington and Williams, 2011), and poor action-potential reliability (McCormick and Prince, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aggelopoulos et al., 1989 and Bourgeois and Rakic, 1993.

claim: Cortical activity during the period of retinal waves follows nearly exactly the macro-patterning of retinal activity: periods of silence lasting 30–60 s are interrupted by 500 ms–2 s waves that occur in clusters lasting up to 10 s.
source: Cortical activity during the period of retinal waves follows nearly exactly the macro-patterning of retinal activity: periods of silence lasting 30–60 s are interrupted by 500 ms–2 s waves that occur in clusters lasting up to 10 s (Hanganu et al., 2006; Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010; Ackman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hanganu et al., 2006; Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010; Ackman et al., 2012.

claim: The cortical activity within waves is organized in rapid 'spindle-burst' oscillations (8–30 Hz).
source: However, the cortical activity within waves is organized in rapid 'spindle-burst' oscillations (8–30 Hz) (Hanganu et al., 2006; Kummer et al., 2016) that are not present in retina and not observed in adult cortical activity, suggesting transitory early circuit properties are responsible for their production (Tolner et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hanganu et al., 2006 and Kummer et al., 2016.

claim: Spindle-bursts are not limited to VC, but are ubiquitous throughout neonatal cortex.
source: Spindle-bursts are not limited to VC, but are ubiquitous throughout neonatal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by general knowledge about neonatal cortical activity patterns.

claim: Spindle-bursts are the rodent homologue of delta-brushes.
source: They are the rodent homologue of delta-brushes (Khazipov et al., 2013a), one of the major components of the human preterm EEG (André et al., 2010), and their absence in patients indicates a poor prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khazipov et al., 2013a.

claim: Delta-brushes are one of the major components of the human preterm EEG.
source: They are the rodent homologue of delta-brushes (Khazipov et al., 2013a), one of the major components of the human preterm EEG (André et al., 2010), and their absence in patients indicates a poor prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to André et al., 2010.

claim: The absence of delta-brushes in patients indicates a poor prognosis.
source: They are the rodent homologue of delta-brushes (Khazipov et al., 2013a), one of the major components of the human preterm EEG (André et al., 2010), and their absence in patients indicates a poor prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by general clinical knowledge about preterm EEG patterns.

claim: Spontaneous activity in VC during the retinal wave period consisted of long periods of network silence interrupted by periods of activity lasting 3–10 s.
source: As previously described (Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010), spontaneous activity in VC during the retinal wave period consisted of long periods of network silence interrupted by periods of activity lasting 3–10 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010 and confirmed by the current study's observations.

claim: Activity within active periods consisted of spindle-shaped oscillations in the local field potential (LFP) in superficial layers with a primary frequency of 20.8 ± 0.8 Hz (n = 7, mean ± SEM).
source: Activity within these active periods consisted of spindle-shaped oscillations in the local field potential (LFP) in superficial layers with a primary frequency of 20.8 ± 0.8 Hz (n = 7, mean ± SEM) and elevated MUA in all layers (Figure 1D,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D,H.

claim: Activity in LGN had a similar structure to VC: 5–10 s periods of spiking activity alternating with periods of low or absent spiking.
source: Activity in LGN had a similar structure: 5–10 s periods of spiking activity alternating with periods of low or absent spiking (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Spike-rate modulation in LGN showed a primary frequency of 23.1 ± 0.6 Hz (n = 7).
source: Spike-rate modulation in LGN showed a primary frequency of 23.1 ± 0.6 Hz (n = 7) (Figure 1G), similar to VC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Spindle-burst oscillations are observed in LGN.
source: Thus, spindle-burst oscillations are also observed in LGN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the frequency analysis of LGN MUA showing oscillations similar to VC.

claim: Retinal silencing dramatically reduced firing rates in LGN (–86.6 ± 3.9%, mean ± SEM) and VC (–67.2 ± 10.2%).
source: As predicted, retinal silencing dramatically reduced firing rates in LGN (–86.6 ± 3.9%, mean ± SEM) and VC (–67.2 ± 10.2%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal silencing experiments.

claim: The continuity of activity was significantly reduced by retinal silencing (LGN –88.5 ± 6.5%, VC –90.6 ± 2.3%).
source: The continuity of activity, measured as the proportion of the recording with spike activity (periods containing at least two spikes with an interval of less than 500 ms, called 'events'), was also significantly reduced (LGN –88.5 ± 6.5%, VC –90.6 ± 2.3%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retinal silencing experiments.

claim: Retinal silencing eliminated events over 5 s in duration in LGN and VC.
source: Examination of the distribution of event lengths after retinal silencing showed that events over 5 s in duration were reduced in LGN and eliminated in VC (Figure 2A4,B4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A4,B4.

claim: Retinal silencing largely eliminated the prominent peak in LGN MUA and VC LFP spectra in the spindle-burst range.
source: Retinal silencing largely eliminated the prominent peak in LGN MUA and VC LFP spectra in the spindle-burst range, leaving only lower frequency activity (Figure 2A5,B5).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 2A5,B5.

claim: In the absence of retinal input, spontaneous activity in the intact thalamocortical loop can provide at most 20% of normal LGN firing.
source: In the absence of retinal input, spontaneous activity in the intact thalamocortical loop can provide at most 20% of normal LGN firing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ~80% reduction in LGN firing after retinal silencing.

claim: Silencing LGN significantly reduced VC L4 MUA rate (–79.0 ± 3.9%) and continuity (–89.0 ± 2.6%).
source: Silencing LGN significantly reduced VC L4 MUA rate (–79.0 ± 3.9%) and continuity (–89.0 ± 2.6%) (Figure 2C3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LGN silencing experiments shown in Figure 2C3.

claim: The remaining VC activity after LGN silencing consisted only of very short bursts (<1 s).
source: The remaining VC activity consisted only of very short bursts (<1 s) (Figure 2C4).
evidence: This claim is supported by event duration analysis shown in Figure 2C4.

claim: LGN silencing completely eliminated oscillatory activity in the VC LFP.
source: Most importantly, LGN silencing completely eliminated oscillatory activity in the VC LFP (Figure 2C5).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 2C5.

claim: VC alone can generate very short bursts of activity, as observed in slices.
source: All of these activity reductions were more severe than observed following retinal silencing; thus while VC alone can generate very short bursts of activity, as observed in slices (Allène et al., 2008), an intact thalamocortical loop is necessary for the generation of activity lasting longer than 1 s that contains any high frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allène et al., 2008 and confirmed by the current study's LGN silencing data.

claim: An intact thalamocortical loop is necessary for the generation of activity lasting longer than 1 s that contains any high frequencies.
source: All of these activity reductions were more severe than observed following retinal silencing; thus while VC alone can generate very short bursts of activity, as observed in slices (Allène et al., 2008), an intact thalamocortical loop is necessary for the generation of activity lasting longer than 1 s that contains any high frequencies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of retinal and LGN silencing effects.

claim: Silencing VC at P9-11 reduces LGN spike-rate by 79.2 ± 5.6% and continuity by 68.4 ± 9.3%.
source: Silencing VC at P9-11 during the peak of stage III waves reduces LGN spike-rate by 79.2 ± 5.6% and continuity by 68.4 ± 9.3% (Figure 3D2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from VC silencing experiments shown in Figure 3D2.

claim: Silencing of either retina or VC results in a greater than 50% reduction in LGN firing, indicating they act synergistically to drive LGN.
source: The fact that silencing of either retina or VC results in a greater than 50% reduction in firing indicates that they act synergistically to drive LGN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of retinal and VC silencing effects on LGN activity.

claim: VC participates in feedback amplification as part of an excitatory loop with LGN that is necessary for the generation of effective thalamic spiking during retinal waves.
source: One explanation is that VC participates in feedback amplification as part of an excitatory loop with LGN that is necessary for the generation of effective thalamic spiking during retinal waves.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the synergistic effects of retinal and VC silencing on LGN activity.

claim: Silencing VC strongly reduced normalized spike spectral power in the spindle-burst range.
source: Silencing VC strongly reduced normalized spike spectral power in the spindle-burst range (Figure 3D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 3D3.

claim: Peak frequency of LGN activity shifted from 24.6 ± 0.9 to 16.2 ± 2.0 Hz after VC silencing.
source: VC input appears to be required for normal patterning of the spindle-oscillations, as peak frequency of remaining activity shifted from 24.6 ± 0.9 to 16.2 ± 2.0 Hz (Figure 3D4) after VC silencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D4.

claim: During the period of peak stage III retinal waves, feedback connections from VC to LGN are a critical component of retinal wave transmission.
source: These results show that during the period of peak stage III retinal waves, feedback connections from VC to LGN are a critical component of retinal wave transmission, which serve to both amplify and prolong spontaneous activity as well as accelerate spindle-burst oscillations in LGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results of VC silencing experiments showing effects on amplitude, duration, and frequency of LGN activity.

claim: Silencing VC at P5-7 significantly reduced LGN spike-rates (−52.0 ± 7.4%) and continuity (−49.8 ± 10.7%).
source: Silencing VC at this age significantly reduced spike-rates (−52.0 ± 7.4%) and continuity (−49.8 ± 10.7%) (Figure 3C2), showing that corticothalamic amplification is present at this age as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from VC silencing experiments at P5-7 shown in Figure 3C2.

claim: There was no significant effect of VC silencing on either spike spectra or event duration at P5-7.
source: However, there was no significant effect of VC silencing on either spike spectra or event duration (Figure 3C3–5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C3-5.

claim: During the first post-natal week, the role of VC is limited to amplification.
source: Thus during the first post-natal week, the role of VC is limited to amplification.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect on spike spectra and event duration despite reduced spike rates at P5-7.

claim: At P5-7, LGN is able to generate spindle-oscillations in response to retinal waves, albeit with a lower frequency than during the second postnatal week.
source: At this age, LGN is able to generate spindle-oscillations in response to retinal waves, albeit with a lower frequency than during the second postnatal week.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of oscillations at P5-7 that are not affected by VC silencing.

claim: Spontaneous activity in VC dramatically changes between P11 and P13.
source: Spontaneous activity in VC dramatically changes between P11 and P13. Cortex no longer exhibits the long silent periods of immaturity; activity becomes continuous and loses the prominent spindle-oscillations, which are replaced by adult-like, broad-band activity (Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010.

claim: VC silencing at P13-14 increases LGN spike rates (+26.2 ± 5.4%).
source: VC silencing at this age does not decrease LGN activity, but rather increases spike rates (+26.2 ± 5.4%) and there is slight but not significant increase in continuity (+13.5 ± 5.0%) (Figure 3E2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from VC silencing experiments at P13-14 shown in Figure 3E2.

claim: VC silencing at P13-14 increases the proportion of very long duration events (>10 s).
source: VC silencing increases the proportion of very long duration events (>10 s) (Figure 3E5), but does not change the LGN MUA spectrum (Figure 3E3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E5.

claim: The excitatory role of corticothalamic feedback is limited to the period of retinal waves, and cortex becomes inhibitory to thalamus around eye-opening.
source: Thus the excitatory role of corticothalamic feedback is limited to the period of retinal waves, and cortex becomes inhibitory to thalamus around eye-opening.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the switch from decreased to increased LGN activity following VC silencing between P9-11 and P13-14.

claim: A 10 ms pulse of 470 nm LED on VC was sufficient to activate deep VC layers at all ages with similar delay (P6-7 3.7 ± 1.8 ms; P9-11 3.4 ± 1.5 ms; P13-14 3.5 ± 1.3 ms).
source: A 10 ms pulse of 470 nm LED on VC was sufficient to activate deep VC layers at all ages with similar delay (P6-7 3.7 ± 1.8 ms; P9-11 3.4 ± 1.5 ms; P13-14 3.5 ± 1.3 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: At all ages, 10 ms light-pulses onto VC evoked short duration (~30 ms) initial spiking in LGN.
source: At all ages, 10 ms light-pulses onto VC evoked short duration (~30 ms) initial spiking in LGN (Figure 4C,D), although the latency to activate LGN following VC activation decreased between P6-7 (34.2 ± 2.7 ms) and P9-11 (21.5 ± 0.5 ms), stabilizing by P13-14 (20.0 ± 0.9 ms) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4C,D,E.

claim: The latency to activate LGN following VC activation decreased between P6-7 (34.2 ± 2.7 ms) and P9-11 (21.5 ± 0.5 ms), stabilizing by P13-14 (20.0 ± 0.9 ms).
source: At all ages, 10 ms light-pulses onto VC evoked short duration (~30 ms) initial spiking in LGN (Figure 4C,D), although the latency to activate LGN following VC activation decreased between P6-7 (34.2 ± 2.7 ms) and P9-11 (21.5 ± 0.5 ms), stabilizing by P13-14 (20.0 ± 0.9 ms) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The probability of generating a spiking response in LGN with each VC activation increased from 39.7 ± 7.0% at P6-7 to 92.4 ± 3.6% at P13-14.
source: The probability of generating a spiking response in LGN with each VC activation increased from 39.7 ± 7.0% at P6-7 to 92.4 ± 3.6% at P13-14 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The major developmental change in the LGN response occurred between P9-11 and P13-14, consisting of the development of post-stimulus inhibition following the initial evoked response.
source: The major developmental change in the LGN response occurred between P9-11 and P13-14. It consisted of the development of post-stimulus inhibition following the initial evoked response (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The relative increase in LGN spike-rates at 100–250 ms after VC stimulation switched from neutral or positive (P6-7 −0.1 ± 36.7%; P9-11 +63.4 ± 61.0%) to negative at P13-14 (−89.2 ± 8.8%).
source: The relative increase in LGN spike-rates at 100–250 ms after VC stimulation switched from neutral or positive (P6-7 −0.1 ± 36.7%; P9-11 +63.4 ± 61.0%) to negative at P13-14 (−89.2 ± 8.8%) indicating the recruitment of functional feedforward inhibition into the corticothalamic circuit between P11 and P13.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: At P6-7, 20 Hz VC stimulation increased LGN spike rates but did not induce oscillatory activity.
source: At P6-7, 20 Hz VC stimulation increased LGN spike rates but did not induce oscillatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patterned optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4I.

claim: At P9-11, 20 Hz VC stimulation induced 20 Hz oscillatory firing in LGN.
source: In contrast, the same stimulation at P9-11 induced 20 Hz oscillatory firing in LGN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patterned optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4I.

claim: At P13-14, despite reliable LGN responses to the first one or two pulses of 20 Hz VC stimulation, induced inhibition prevented further oscillation.
source: At P13-14, despite reliable LGN responses to the first one or two pulses, induced inhibition prevented further oscillation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patterned optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 4I.

claim: During the second postnatal week when glutamatergic waves predominate (P9-11), increasing speed and reliability of the feedback loop enables cortex to synchronize LGN at higher frequencies than LGN alone would naturally oscillate.
source: Then during the second postnatal week when glutamatergic waves predominate (P9-11), increasing speed and reliability of the feedback loop enables cortex to synchronize LGN at higher frequencies than LGN alone would naturally oscillate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of VC silencing and optogenetic stimulation data showing frequency shifts and entrainment.

claim: At the transition to the third week (after P13), VC afferents recruit an inhibitory circuit, which reduces their ability to synchronize activity at high frequencies and makes the net effect of corticothalamic feedback inhibitory.
source: Finally, at the transition to the third week (after P13), VC afferents recruit an inhibitory circuit, which reduces their ability to synchronize activity at high frequencies and makes the net effect of corticothalamic feedback inhibitory, as in the adult.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the development of post-stimulus inhibition and the switch to net inhibitory effects of VC on LGN.

claim: P9-11 LGN visual responses consisted of early-gamma (30–50 Hz) followed by spindle-burst oscillations (8–30 Hz).
source: P9-11 LGN visual responses also consisted of early-gamma (30–50 Hz) followed by spindle-burst oscillations (8–30 Hz) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from visual stimulation experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Silencing VC reduced spike rates in LGN during both the primary and secondary visual responses (−46.2 ± 4.8% and −48.7 ± 5.8% respectively).
source: Silencing VC reduced spike rates in LGN during both the primary and secondary responses (−46.2 ± 4.8% and −48.7 ± 5.8% respectively) (Figure 5D,F), but reduced the power of spike-rate oscillations only for spindle-burst oscillations (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from VC silencing during visual stimulation shown in Figure 5D,F.

claim: VC silencing reduced the power of spike-rate oscillations only for spindle-burst oscillations, not for early-gamma oscillations.
source: Silencing VC reduced spike rates in LGN during both the primary and secondary responses (−46.2 ± 4.8% and −48.7 ± 5.8% respectively) (Figure 5D,F), but reduced the power of spike-rate oscillations only for spindle-burst oscillations (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Corticothalamic excitation is specifically implicated in the generation of spindle-bursts, but not EGOs.
source: These results confirm the strong amplification role of early corticothalamic feedback, and specifically implicate corticothalamic excitation in the generation of spindle-bursts, but not EGOs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of VC silencing on spindle-burst versus EGO oscillations.

claim: At P13-14 visual responses in LGN were shorter and consisted of a rapid, non-oscillatory primary response, and greatly reduced secondary response.
source: At P13-14 visual responses in LGN were shorter and consisted of a rapid, non-oscillatory primary response, and greatly reduced secondary response (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Silencing VC at P13-14 caused a non-significant increase in the evoked spike-rate during the primary response (+15.1 ± 13.3%) and a significant increase in the secondary response (+48.5 ± 9.0%).
source: As observed for spontaneous activity, silencing VC at this age no longer reduced LGN activity. Instead, it caused a non-significant increase in the evoked spike-rate during the primary response (+15.1 ± 13.3%) and a significant increase in the secondary response (+48.5 ± 9.0%) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The switch in corticothalamic feedback from functionally excitatory to inhibitory is not limited to spontaneous activity.
source: These results show that the switch in corticothalamic feedback from functionally excitatory to inhibitory is not limited to spontaneous activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar effects of VC silencing on both spontaneous and evoked activity at P13-14.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback is not necessary for the loss of evoked gamma and spindle-bursts from visual responses at P13.
source: They further show that corticothalamic feedback is not necessary for the loss of evoked gamma and spindle-bursts from visual responses at P13, which instead appear to depend on altered circuitry in LGN and retina.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that oscillations are lost at P13 despite the presence of corticothalamic feedback.

claim: Before vision, when spontaneous retinal waves instruct circuit formation, the corticothalamic projection provides excitatory feedback amplification to thalamus.
source: Before vision, when spontaneous retinal waves instruct circuit formation (Huberman et al., 2008), the corticothalamic projection provides excitatory feedback amplification to thalamus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results of pharmacological silencing and optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Retinal waves alone provide as little as 20% of the total drive to LGN.
source: Although retina initiates activity in central visual circuits, retinal waves alone provide as little as 20% of the total drive.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the residual activity remaining after retinal silencing.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback amplification accounts for approximately 80% of LGN drive during retinal waves.
source: Corticothalamic feedback amplification accounts for the remaining 80%, effectively gating transmission of retinal waves in thalamus.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the large reduction in LGN activity following VC silencing.

claim: During the second post-natal week corticothalamic excitation not only amplifies, but also synchronizes, thalamic firing.
source: During the second post-natal week corticothalamic excitation not only amplifies, but also synchronizes, thalamic firing, effectively conditioning its own input.
evidence: This claim is supported by the frequency shift and entrainment data from VC silencing and optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The mechanism of transient corticothalamic excitation is the delayed development of inhibitory recruitment by the corticothalamic projection.
source: The mechanism is the delayed development of inhibitory recruitment by the corticothalamic projection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the development of post-stimulus inhibition between P9-11 and P13-14.

claim: Neither VC alone, nor an intact LGN-VC loop, is capable of producing more than brief bursts of activity.
source: Neither VC alone, nor an intact LGN-VC loop, is capable of producing more than brief bursts of activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the LGN silencing data showing elimination of long-duration events in VC.

claim: Without VC, firing in LGN is dramatically reduced but sustained activity is still present.
source: In contrast, without VC, firing in LGN is dramatically reduced but sustained activity is still present.
evidence: This claim is supported by the VC silencing data showing reduced but not eliminated LGN activity.

claim: Only the longest events in LGN—caused by sustained firing between waves occurring in a cluster—are suppressed by VC silencing.
source: Only the longest events—caused by sustained firing between waves occurring in a cluster (Blankenship and Feller, 2010)—are suppressed by VC silencing, demonstrating that corticothalamic feedback maintains activity during waves but does not initiate activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the event duration analysis from VC silencing experiments and citation to Blankenship and Feller, 2010.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback maintains activity during waves but does not initiate activity.
source: Only the longest events—caused by sustained firing between waves occurring in a cluster (Blankenship and Feller, 2010)—are suppressed by VC silencing, demonstrating that corticothalamic feedback maintains activity during waves but does not initiate activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of event duration changes following VC silencing.

claim: VC makes a feed-forward excitatory loop with thalamus that amplifies the drive from retina.
source: Together our findings suggest that VC makes a feed-forward excitatory loop with thalamus that amplifies the drive from retina.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the multiplicative effects of retinal and VC silencing on LGN activity.

claim: In ferrets corticothalamic feedback synchronizes activity between eye-specific lamina.
source: In ferrets corticothalamic feedback synchronizes activity between eye-specific lamina (Weliky and Katz, 1999), but its role in amplification and oscillation generation is unknown, as is whether this function is unique to rodents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weliky and Katz, 1999.

claim: Almost all activity in early VC occurs as rapid oscillations necessary for synaptic stabilization in the developing circuit.
source: Almost all activity in early VC, as well as every other cortical region examined, occurs as rapid oscillations necessary for synaptic stabilization in the developing circuit (Khazipov et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Khazipov et al., 2013a, 2013b.

claim: In all cortical areas, rapid oscillations occur in response to spontaneous and evoked firing of the dominant input, with a frequency inversely proportional to its temporal and spatial specificity.
source: In all areas, rapid oscillations occur in response to spontaneous and evoked firing of the dominant input (eg. whisker in barrel cortex), with a frequency inversely proportional to its temporal and spatial specificity (Khazipov et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khazipov et al., 2013b.

claim: LGN is the locus of generation of VC spindle-bursts, similar to somatosensory (VPN) thalamus.
source: Here we identify LGN as the locus of generation of VC spindle-bursts, similar to somatosensory (VPN) thalamus (Yang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citation to Yang et al., 2013a.

claim: Unlike VPN, corticothalamic feedback plays a critical role for setting the frequency and amplitude of LGN firing.
source: Unlike VPN, corticothalamic feedback plays a critical role for setting the frequency and amplitude of LGN firing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of the current results with previous findings in somatosensory thalamus.

claim: During the first post-natal week, corticothalamic connections are capable of directly driving LGN, but only at long latency and with poor reliability.
source: During the first post-natal week, corticothalamic connections are capable of directly driving LGN, but only at long latency and with poor reliability, consistent with their low density in LGN at this age (Seabrook et al., 2013; Grant et al., 2016), and they are not necessary for rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic stimulation data and citations to Seabrook et al., 2013 and Grant et al., 2016.

claim: Between the first and second post-natal weeks, the timing and reliability of corticothalamic connectivity improves, changing its role from simple amplification to synchronization and rhythmogenesis.
source: Between the first and second post-natal weeks, roughly synchronized to the switch between cholinergic and glutamatergic waves (Huberman et al., 2008), the timing and reliability of corticothalamic connectivity improves, changing its role from simple amplification to synchronization and rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the developmental changes in latency, reliability, and functional effects observed in optogenetic and silencing experiments.

claim: LGN can generate its own weak (15 Hz) oscillations in the first week, but requires VC to generate normal (25 Hz) activity in the second week.
source: LGN can still generate its own weak (15 Hz) oscillations in the first week, but it requires VC to generate normal (25 Hz) activity in the second week.
evidence: This claim is supported by the frequency analysis data from VC silencing experiments at different ages.

claim: The faster spindle-burst oscillations are generated in the feedback circuit between LGN and VC.
source: Because corticothalamic projections are only capable of synchronizing LGN at these frequencies at this age (Figure 4), and L5/6 neurons are synchronized by the spindle-oscillations (Colonnese and Khazipov, 2010), we suggest that the faster spindle-burst oscillations are generated in the feedback circuit between the two structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of optogenetic entrainment data and previous observations of L5/6 synchronization.

claim: The role of corticothalamic feedback appears specific to spindle-bursts, as it is not important for the generation of Early-Gamma Oscillations (EGOs).
source: The role of corticothalamic feedback appears specific to spindle-bursts, as it is not important for the generation of the other major early oscillation, Early-Gamma Oscillations (EGOs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential effects of VC silencing on spindle-burst versus EGO oscillations during visual responses.

claim: EGOs activate only the input and superficial layers of a single column, and occur only in response to temporally and spatially limited input.
source: In contrast to spindle-bursts, EGOs activate only the input and superficial layers of a single column, and occur only in response to temporally and spatially limited input (Khazipov et al., 2013b), for example in response to a single deflection of the principle whisker in barrel cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Khazipov et al., 2013b.

claim: VC EGOs do not occur in response to retinal waves, but can be induced by visual stimulation.
source: VC EGOs do not occur in response to retinal waves, but can be induced by visual stimulation (Colonnese et al., 2010), allowing us to examine their cortical dependence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colonnese et al., 2010.

claim: While LGN spiking during the period of EGOs was reduced by VC silencing, the normalized oscillation power was unaffected.
source: While LGN spiking during the period of EGOs was reduced by VC silencing, the normalized oscillation power was unaffected, suggesting that VC provides amplification but not rhythmogenesis for EGOs.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data from visual response experiments with VC silencing.

claim: Poor modulation of EGOs by corticothalamic projections is consistent with the conduction delays (>20 ms) and lack of L5/6 firing during EGOs.
source: Poor modulation of EGOs by corticothalamic projections is consistent with the conduction delays (>20 ms) and lack of L5/6 firing during EGOs (Colonnese et al., 2010) which should prevent corticothalamic projections from contributing to such rapid synchronization of LGN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing constraints and previous observations cited from Colonnese et al., 2010.

claim: In barrel cortex, cortical silencing reduces frequency power for EGOs but not spindle-bursts.
source: In barrel cortex, cortical silencing reduces frequency power for EGOs but not spindle-bursts (Yang et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2013a.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback may be differentially tuned by region, as EGOs occur spontaneously in barrel-cortex but not in VC.
source: Thus corticothalamic feedback may be differentially tuned by region, as EGOs occur spontaneously in barrel-cortex but not in VC (Yang et al., 2009; Cichon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of results across cortical regions and supported by citations to Yang et al., 2009 and Cichon et al., 2014.

claim: Defective transient circuits can disrupt circuit formation and then disappear, leaving no trace in the adult.
source: Defective transient circuits can disrupt circuit formation and then disappear, leaving no trace in the adult.
evidence: This claim is based on general principles of developmental neuroscience.

claim: Failure to reorganize early circuits into their mature configurations is a likely cause of adult dysfunction.
source: Failure to reorganize early circuits into their mature configurations is another likely cause of adult dysfunction (Ben-Ari, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ben-Ari, 2008.

claim: Important transitional synaptic properties include elevated input resistance, long duration NMDA currents with poor Mg++ block, glutamate spillover, and plateau potentials.
source: Important transitional synaptic properties include elevated input resistance, long duration NMDA currents with poor Mg++ block, glutamate spillover, and plateau potentials (Lo et al., 2002; Hauser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lo et al., 2002 and Hauser et al., 2014.

claim: Transitional circuits include early-born subplate neurons and L5 somatostatin neurons, both of which receive early thalamocortical synapses.
source: Transitional circuits include early-born subplate neurons and L5 somatostatin neurons, both of which receive early thalamocortical synapses (Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016.

claim: Amplification involves functional strength that seems larger than that predicted given VC terminal density.
source: Amplification involves functional strength that seems larger than that predicted given VC terminal density (Seabrook et al., 2013; Grant et al., 2016), but also the late integration of inhibition into the circuit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of functional effects with anatomical observations cited from Seabrook et al., 2013 and Grant et al., 2016.

claim: The source of corticothalamic feedback could include contributions from the normal L6 projection as well as L5, whose axons traverse LGN without extensive arborization due to competition from retinal axons.
source: The source of corticothalamic feedback could include contributions from the normal L6 projection as well as L5, whose axons traverse LGN without extensive arborization due to competition from retinal axons (Grant et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Grant et al., 2016.

claim: Corticothalamic feedback is a potential contributor to circuit refinements that are dependent on retinal waves in LGN and cortex.
source: Our results identify corticothalamic feedback as a potential contributor to circuit refinements that are dependent on retinal waves in LGN and cortex (Huberman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the current results and citation to Huberman et al., 2008.

claim: The amplification identified here likely contributes to the defects in retinal ganglion cell targeting caused by genetic ablation of cortex.
source: The amplification identified here likely contributes to the defects in retinal ganglion cell targeting caused by genetic ablation of cortex (Shanks et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Shanks et al., 2016.

claim: The prominent role of corticothalamic feedback in patterning LGN responses to glutamatergic waves suggests it is particularly critical for synaptic refinement driven by these waves.
source: The prominent role of corticothalamic feedback in patterning LGN responses to glutamatergic waves suggests it is particularly critical for synaptic refinement driven by these waves.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the differential effects at different developmental stages.

claim: Perturbation of glutamatergic waves reduces segregation of C-lamina and maintenance of A-lamina segregation in LGN.
source: The role of glutamatergic waves remains controversial (Kerschensteiner, 2016), but their perturbation reduces segregation of C-lamina and maintenance of A-lamina segregation in LGN (Davis et al., 2015a, 2015b) as well as orientation selectivity in VC (Huberman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2015a, 2015b and Huberman et al., 2008.

claim: A similar near doubling of occipital delta-brush frequencies occurs in human infants between 27 and 35 gestational weeks.
source: A similar near doubling of occipital delta-brush frequencies occurs in human infants between 27 and 35 gestational weeks (André et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to André et al., 2010.

claim: Acceleration of early oscillations is a conserved feature of cortical development.
source: Thus, acceleration of early oscillations is a conserved feature of cortical development, for which we have identified a mechanism.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of rodent and human developmental patterns.

claim: Driving cortical inputs at 10 Hz causes synaptic depression in immature somatosensory cortex at age equivalents, while higher frequencies cause potentiation.
source: Driving cortical inputs at 10 Hz causes synaptic depression in immature somatosensory cortex at age equivalents (Minlebaev et al., 2011), while higher frequencies cause potentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Minlebaev et al., 2011.

claim: The acceleration in oscillation frequency may be a function of the change from 'burst-based' plasticity rules used to grossly align topography to more precise spike-timing dependent plasticity.
source: Thus the acceleration in oscillation frequency may be a function of the change from 'burst-based' plasticity rules used to grossly align topography (Butts et al., 2007), to more precise spike-timing dependent plasticity that can take advantage of the increasing specificity of firing patterns within retinal waves (Kerschensteiner and Wong, 2008) to reduce poly-innervation of relay cells (Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005) and refine orientation selectivity (Huberman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Butts et al., 2007; Kerschensteiner and Wong, 2008; Jaubert-Miazza et al., 2005; and Huberman et al., 2008.

claim: Thalamocortical circuits function as an integrated circuit even during early development.
source: Overall our results show that thalamocortical circuits function as an integrated circuit even during early development, and suggest that spontaneous retinal activity influences the development of corticothalamic feedback to LGN and reticular thalamus (RT).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results showing interdependence of LGN and VC activity.

claim: Spontaneous retinal activity influences the development of corticothalamic feedback to LGN and reticular thalamus (RT).
source: Overall our results show that thalamocortical circuits function as an integrated circuit even during early development, and suggest that spontaneous retinal activity influences the development of corticothalamic feedback to LGN and reticular thalamus (RT).
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the developmental changes observed.

claim: For driver inputs, feedforward inhibition develops later than excitation, but their functional effect remains excitatory.
source: For drivers, feedforward inhibition develops later than excitation (Ziburkus et al., 2003; Colonnese, 2014), but their functional effect remains excitatory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ziburkus et al., 2003 and Colonnese, 2014.

claim: For a modulator pathway, its role during development is different from its role in the adult, switching from an excitatory and amplifying role early, to a modulatory, net-inhibitory role later.
source: Here we show that for a modulator its role during development is different from its role in the adult, switching from an excitatory and amplifying role early, to a modulatory, net-inhibitory role later.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results of silencing and optogenetic experiments across developmental ages.

claim: This principle may apply to other modulatory feedback projections, such as intra-cortical feedback, which largely synapse on interneurons and develop later than feedforward connections.
source: This principle may apply to other modulatory feedback projections, such as intra-cortical feedback, which largely synapse on interneurons and develop later than feedforward connections (Berezovskii et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Berezovskii et al., 2011 and Yang et al., 2013b.

claim: The lack of thalamocortical feedback inhibition has implications for seizure susceptibility during infancy.
source: The lack of thalamocortical feedback inhibition has implications for seizure susceptibility during infancy, because thalamocortical synchronization through RT is an important mechanism of seizure spread (Paz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Paz et al., 2013.

claim: Preterm infants and neonates are highly susceptible to seizures.
source: Preterm infants and neonates are highly susceptible to seizures (Rakhade and Jensen, 2009), and excitatory feedback amplification through thalamus may amplify paroxysmal events.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rakhade and Jensen, 2009.

claim: Excitatory feedback amplification through thalamus may amplify paroxysmal events.
source: Preterm infants and neonates are highly susceptible to seizures (Rakhade and Jensen, 2009), and excitatory feedback amplification through thalamus may amplify paroxysmal events.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the current findings about excitatory feedback.

claim: Lack of inhibitory recruitment by cortex likely contributes to the differences in frequency and propagation of neonatal seizures.
source: Conversely, lack of inhibitory recruitment by cortex likely contributes to the differences in frequency and propagation of neonatal seizures.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the current findings.

claim: The mechanism by which functional corticothalamic inhibition develops between P11 and P13 likely involves the recruitment of RT, and not LGN, interneurons.
source: The mechanism by which functional corticothalamic inhibition develops between P11 and P13 likely involves the recruitment of RT, and not LGN, interneurons, as they are poorly driven by VC (Jurgens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Jurgens et al., 2012.

claim: It is unlikely that the development of functional corticothalamic inhibition is due to a change in the polarity of GABAA currents, as GABA is inhibitory in LGN during the first post-natal week.
source: It is also unlikely to be due to a change in the polarity of GABAA currents, as GABA is inhibitory in LGN during the first post-natal week.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about GABA polarity development.

claim: Feedforward inhibition in both VC and LGN is potentiated between P11 and P13.
source: Feedforward inhibition in both VC and LGN is potentiated between P11 and P13 (Lo et al., 2002; Colonnese, 2014), suggesting a common factor is responsible.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lo et al., 2002 and Colonnese, 2014.

claim: One prominent candidate for the common factor responsible for inhibitory potentiation includes an increase in continuous activity driven by midbrain neuromodulatory inputs and/or spontaneous non-wave retinal activity.
source: One prominent candidate for future work includes an increase in continuous activity driven by midbrain neuromodulatory inputs (Colonnese et al., 2010) and/or spontaneous non-wave retinal activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citation to Colonnese et al., 2010.

claim: A high excitatory to inhibitory ratio during development has been suggested to compensate for low synaptic density.
source: A high excitatory to inhibitory ratio during development has been suggested to compensate for low synaptic density (Le Magueresse and Monyer, 2013), however a clear correlation with specific developmental events is lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Le Magueresse and Monyer, 2013.

claim: By showing a strong contribution to corticothalamic gating of retinal waves, we establish a specific role for late inhibitory development.
source: By showing a strong contribution to corticothalamic gating of retinal waves, we establish a specific role for late inhibitory development, and provide potential experimental predictions to test its role in circuit formation.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main contribution of the current study.

claim: Injection of AAV-Chronos-GFP into VC at P0-1 yielded strong expression in VC neurons in all layers and axon terminals by P6.
source: Injection of AAV-Chronos-GFP into VC at P0-1 yielded strong expression in VC neurons in all layers and axon terminals by P6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In neonatal mice cortical axons avoid LGN relative to surrounding thalamic nuclei.
source: In neonatal mice (Seabrook et al., 2013; Grant et al., 2016) cortical axons avoid LGN relative to surrounding thalamic nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Seabrook et al., 2013 and Grant et al., 2016.

claim: The same pattern of cortical axon avoidance of LGN was observed in VC axons expressing Chronos-GFP.
source: We observed the same pattern in VC axons expressing Chronos-GFP (Figure 4B), although cortical axon arbors can be seen within LGN even at P6.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Eyelid opening occurred between P13 and P14.
source: Eyelid opening occurred between P13 and P14.
evidence: This is a standard developmental observation in rats.
